title: Ending with dignity
hookLine: a divorce document, and a hope for kindness on both sides

cards: A scribe dips a quill. Around the table sit a rabbinic court of three and two witnesses, and across from them, two people who once stood under a canopy together.
The scribe writes a short document by hand, on purpose, for this one couple, their names spelled out with care. It is folded, then placed into her hands, and she takes it. That is all.
No shouting, no verdict about who was right. Jewish law knows that some marriages end. The question it keeps asking is how.

teach.b: The document is called a get, and its root is in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the old Jewish Publication Society translation describes a husband who "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand."
It is written. A divorce in Jewish law isn't a mood or a slammed door; it's a careful act before witnesses, so no one is left wondering whether they are free. Clarity is its own kind of kindness.
It is given into a hand: the ending happens person to person. In traditional law the husband gives and the wife receives, and both must do it willingly. And the sorrow is allowed.
The prophet Malachi has God say, "For I hate putting away."

The Talmud adds a picture some readers never forget: when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears. Divorce is permitted, and it is still a loss worth grieving. Now the hard part, said plainly.
Because the get must be given freely, a spouse can refuse to give it, and a woman can be left unable to remarry. She is called an agunah, a chained woman.

Rabbis and communities have worked on this for a long time, and today some couples sign agreements before the wedding so that no one is ever trapped. Underneath it all is a hope: kindness on both sides, even at the end.
A marriage that began with blessings can close with honesty, clear words, and no one humiliated.

how: In traditional Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a divorce document written by a scribe and given by the husband to the wife before a rabbinic court and witnesses; some couples today also sign a prenuptial agreement meant to ensure a get is never withheld.

ending a marriage clearly, kindly, with no one trapped

games.why: the Talmud says the altar sheds tears over a man who divorces the wife of his youth: permitted, and still a loss.

practice: Bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or should: a job, a habit, a friendship that has run its course.
Ask, a few breaths apart: is the ending clear, is it person to person rather than a vanishing act, and is there anything kind I could still say?
Let one honest, gentle sentence form, and if you pray, hold the people on the other side of that ending in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ending with dignity. A get written by hand, given into a hand, a loss allowed to be a loss, and no one left chained. Today's word.
